questions.q: A GHS-compliant Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is organized into how many sections?
questions.e: The standardized SDS format has 16 numbered sections.

questions.q: The two GHS signal words are:
questions.e: 'Danger' is used for more severe hazard categories, 'Warning' for less severe ones.

questions.q: A GHS pictogram showing a flame over a circle indicates:
questions.e: Flame over circle = oxidizer (can intensify fire). A plain flame = flammable.

questions.q: Which SDS section lists exposure limits and recommended personal protective equipment?
questions.e: Section 8 covers occupational exposure limits, engineering controls and PPE; Section 4 gives first-aid measures.

questions.q: On a GHS label, 'H' codes and 'P' codes stand for:
questions.e: H-statements describe the nature of the hazard; P-statements recommend measures to prevent or respond to exposure.

questions.q: You receive an unfamiliar chemical. Name at least five SDS items you would check before using or storing it, and why.
questions.m: Section 2 (hazard identification: pictograms, classes, H/P-statements); Section 4 (first-aid); Section 5 (firefighting: suitable extinguishing media); Section 7 (handling and storage, incompatibilities); Section 8 (exposure limits, engineering controls, PPE); Section 9 (physical properties: flash point, vapor pressure); Section 10 (stability and reactivity: incompatible materials, hazardous decomposition); Section 11 (toxicological information); Section 13 (disposal). The goal is to anticipate hazards, define controls and plan for emergencies before opening the container.

questions.q: The LD50 of a substance is:
c: The dose that kills 50% of a test population; a lower LD50 means higher acute toxicity
The dose that is safe for 50% of people
The concentration in air that causes odor in 50% of people
The dose at which half of the substance is excreted
questions.e: LD50 is a statistical acute-lethality measure, typically in mg/kg body weight.

questions.q: Substance A has an oral LD50 of 5 mg/kg and substance B has 500 mg/kg (same species). Which is more acutely toxic by ingestion?
questions.e: Less substance is needed to cause the same lethal effect.

questions.q: The main routes by which chemicals enter the body in a workplace are:
c: Inhalation, skin/eye absorption, ingestion and injection
questions.e: Controls need to address every plausible route, not just inhalation.

questions.q: Which exposure limit must never be exceeded at any moment?
questions.e: TWA averages over a shift, STEL is a 15-minute average, ceiling is an instantaneous maximum.

questions.q: Why is odor an unreliable warning property for some toxic gases (for example hydrogen sulfide)?
questions.m: Olfactory fatigue (the nose adapts and stops detecting the gas), and at high concentrations some gases paralyze the sense of smell, so absence of smell does not mean absence of hazard. Odor thresholds also vary between individuals and may be above the permissible exposure limit for some chemicals, so detection should rely on instruments and exposure limits, not on smell.

questions.q: Acute toxicity differs from chronic toxicity in that chronic toxicity:
c: Results from repeated or long-term exposure, often at lower doses
Occurs only after a single large exposure
Cannot be harmful at low exposure
questions.e: Examples: carcinogenicity, organ damage and sensitization may appear long after exposure began.

questions.q: Why must household bleach (sodium hypochlorite) never be mixed with ammonia-based cleaners?
c: They react to form toxic chloramine vapors
questions.e: Hypochlorite and ammonia form chloramines, which are respiratory irritants and toxic.

questions.q: Mixing bleach with an acidic cleaner is dangerous because it:
questions.e: Acidifying hypochlorite shifts chemistry toward Cl₂, a toxic irritant gas.

questions.q: Strong oxidizers (nitrates, peroxides, chlorates) are stored away from organic solvents and fuels because:
c: The oxidizer supplies oxygen, so a fuel can burn or react violently without air
questions.e: A fire normally needs fuel, oxidizer and ignition; an oxidizer in contact with fuel removes the dependence on atmospheric oxygen.

questions.q: Why are cyanide or sulfide salts never stored or handled together with acids?
c: Acids convert them to volatile toxic gases (HCN or H₂S)
Acids oxidize them to harmless oxides
questions.e: Protonation of CN⁻ and S²⁻ yields hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen sulfide, both highly toxic gases.

questions.q: Water-reactive metals such as sodium or potassium are hazardous around water because:
c: The reaction releases flammable hydrogen and enough heat to ignite it
questions.e: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ is strongly exothermic.

questions.q: When diluting concentrated sulfuric acid you should add:
c: Acid slowly to water, with stirring and cooling
Both at once in a closed bottle
Acid to a dry beaker, then add water
questions.e: The large heat of dilution can boil water locally and spatter; adding acid to a larger volume of water keeps heat absorbed.

questions.q: Explain conceptually why ethers such as diethyl ether and THF are classified as peroxide-forming solvents and how the risk is managed.
questions.m: On exposure to air and light, ethers undergo slow autoxidation (radical chain) forming hydroperoxides and peroxides that are not volatile and can concentrate when the solvent is evaporated or distilled, becoming shock- and heat-sensitive. Controls: buy small quantities, date containers on receipt and opening, use inhibitor-containing grades, store sealed in the dark, test before concentrating, never evaporate to dryness, and dispose of old or crystal-containing containers through hazardous-waste specialists without opening or moving them.

questions.q: A thermal runaway occurs when:
c: Heat generation exceeds heat removal and the imbalance grows because reaction rate rises exponentially with temperature
The reaction stops because of product inhibition
questions.e: Arrhenius dependence makes generation rise faster than the roughly linear removal.

questions.q: A semi-batch reactor is fed reagent faster than it reacts, so unreacted reagent accumulates. The hazard is that:
c: If cooling is lost or reaction suddenly starts, the accumulated reagent can react rapidly, releasing stored energy
The product concentration becomes too low
questions.e: Feed-controlled (non-accumulating) operation limits the energy available for a runaway.

questions.q: A 1.0 mol/L aqueous solution undergoes a reaction with −ΔH = 100 kJ/mol. Taking the heat capacity as 4.18 J/(mL·K), the adiabatic temperature rise is about:
Scaling a reaction up from a flask to a large vessel increases runaway risk mainly because:
c: Heat generation scales with volume while heat removal scales with area, so the surface-to-volume ratio falls
questions.e: Volume ∝ L³ but jacket area ∝ L².

questions.q: Using heat-generation G(T) and heat-removal R(T) curves, state the stability condition for a steady operating point and what happens when it is lost.
questions.m: A steady state is where G(T) = R(T). It is stable only if, at that point, dR/dT > dG/dT (a small temperature rise removes more heat than it generates, restoring the state). If dG/dT exceeds dR/dT (for example after losing cooling, raising feed temperature, or adding reactant too fast), a small positive deviation grows and the temperature climbs toward a high-temperature steady state or beyond safe limits: thermal runaway.

questions.q: The flash point of a liquid is:
c: The lowest temperature at which it gives off enough vapor to form an ignitable mixture with air near its surface
The temperature at which it boils
The temperature at which it ignites spontaneously
The temperature at which it freezes
questions.e: Lower flash point means a more easily ignited liquid.

questions.q: The lower explosion limit (LEL) is the:
c: Minimum vapor concentration in air that can propagate a flame
Maximum vapor concentration in air that can burn
questions.e: Below the LEL the mixture is too lean; above the UEL it is too rich.

questions.q: Methane is flammable in air at roughly:
questions.e: LEL ≈ 5%, UEL ≈ 15% for methane in air at room temperature.

questions.q: The autoignition temperature of a substance is the temperature at which:
c: It ignites without an external ignition source
It decomposes in an inert atmosphere only
questions.e: A hot surface above this temperature can ignite the mixture.

questions.q: In addition to fuel, oxidizer and ignition (the fire triangle), a dust explosion requires:
c: Dispersion of the dust in air and confinement
questions.e: Dispersion gives a high surface area cloud; confinement lets pressure build.

questions.q: Vapors of most flammable liquids are heavier than air, so they tend to:
c: Accumulate at low points and travel to distant ignition sources
questions.e: This is why ignition sources must be controlled well beyond the immediate area of a spill.

questions.q: Explain how nitrogen inerting and grounding/bonding reduce ignition hazards when transferring flammable liquids.
questions.m: Inerting lowers the oxygen concentration below the limiting oxygen concentration so the vapor space cannot support combustion even if an ignition source appears. Flowing liquids and powders generate static charge; bonding connects conductive items so they are at the same potential and grounding drains charge to earth, preventing spark discharges with energy above the minimum ignition energy of the vapor.

questions.q: In the hierarchy of controls, from most to least effective, the order is:
c: Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE
PPE, administrative controls, engineering controls, substitution, elimination
Administrative controls, PPE, elimination, substitution, engineering
questions.e: PPE is the last line of defense because it relies on human behavior and only protects the wearer.

questions.q: A chemical fume hood is an example of:
questions.e: It removes vapors at the source.

questions.q: Following chemical contact with the eyes, the eyes should be flushed at an eyewash station for at least:
questions.e: Standards call for a continuous 15-minute flush, followed by medical evaluation.

questions.q: Glove choice for a particular solvent should be based on:
c: The glove material's breakthrough/permeation data for that chemical
Whether it fits in the pocket
questions.e: No glove material resists all chemicals; manufacturers publish permeation charts.

questions.q: On discovering a chemical spill, the first priority is to:
c: Protect people: alert others, move away from exposure and consult the SDS before deciding if you can safely respond
Wipe it up immediately with paper towels
questions.e: Responders should only clean up spills they are trained and equipped for; otherwise evacuate and call emergency support.

questions.q: State the general first-response principles for skin exposure to a corrosive liquid.
questions.m: Move the person out of the hazard; use the safety shower or running water immediately; remove contaminated clothing and jewelry while flushing; flush for at least 15 minutes; do not apply neutralizing agents unless the SDS says so; seek medical attention and give responders the SDS; report the incident so the cause can be corrected.

questions.q: A HAZOP study is carried out by:
c: A multidisciplinary team applying guide words to process parameters at each node of the P&ID
One operator walking around the plant
questions.e: Deviations such as no flow, more pressure, or less temperature are examined for causes and consequences.

questions.q: A pressure relief valve primarily protects equipment against:
questions.e: It opens at its set pressure to vent and prevent vessel rupture; it is the last layer of protection.

questions.q: Inherently safer design aims to:
c: Remove or reduce the hazard itself (minimize, substitute, moderate, simplify) rather than only control it with add-on safeguards
Add more alarms to existing hazards
Rely on PPE for all workers
questions.e: Hazards that are eliminated cannot fail; hazards that are controlled can.

questions.q: The 1974 Flixborough disaster is a standard case study mainly for the lesson that:
c: Temporary plant modifications need formal engineering review (management of change)
questions.e: A temporary bypass pipe was installed without adequate design review and failed, releasing a large flammable vapor cloud.

questions.q: Using the 1984 Bhopal methyl isocyanate release as a case, explain how inherently safer design and layers of protection apply.
questions.m: A large inventory of a highly toxic, reactive intermediate was stored; a contaminated tank reacted exothermically and several protective layers (refrigeration, scrubber, flare, alarms) were degraded or out of service. Inherently safer design would minimize inventory (make-and-use on demand) or substitute a less hazardous route, removing the possibility of a catastrophic release. Layers of protection need independence, maintenance, and management oversight; if several layers are disabled together the residual risk is far greater than assumed.
